query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Coating as-cast HfNbTaTiZr with a thin, alumina-forming Al-rich layer will significantly improve its oxidation resistance at high temperatures without compromising its intrinsic ductility and yield strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in its as-cast state with 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility and yield strength in the range of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Apply a submicron Al-rich coating via pack cementation or physical vapor deposition.
generation.conditions: Exposure at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere for durations of 100–500 hours under strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a coherent and resistant Al2O3 scale at the alloy's surface.
generation.mechanism: Upon initial heating, the Al-rich coating oxidizes to form a stable and adherent Al2O3 barrier that slows oxygen diffusion into the bulk. This protective layer minimizes oxidation-induced damage at grain boundaries without altering the underlying microstructure that imparts the alloy's favorable mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated alloy is expected to display markedly reduced oxygen uptake and oxidation-induced embrittlement during high-temperature exposure while maintaining its room-temperature tensile ductility and high-temperature yield strength similar to the untreated material.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-cast HfNbTaTiZr, which exhibits poor oxygen resistance leading to degradation during high-temperature exposure.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to high-temperature applications (around 1000 °C) in oxidizing environments with exposure times relevant to prolonged service (100–500 hours) and under mechanical loading with strain rates of 10^−4–10^−2 s^−1.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adherence and integrity of the Al2O3 scale under cyclic thermal-mechanical stresses remains to be fully quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of as-cast HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one group with the applied Al-rich coating and an uncoated control group. Expose both groups to 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere for 500 hours. Following exposure, perform high-temperature tensile tests (with strain rates between 10^−4 and 10^−2 s^−1) and compare oxygen uptake through weight gain and surface analysis.
measurements: Weight gain measurements (to assess oxidation rate)
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (using SEM or TEM) to verify Al2O3 scale formation and integrity
Mechanical property tests (yield strength and ductility) at high temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alumina-coated specimens do not show a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake or demonstrate a decrease in mechanical performance (yield strength or ductility) compared to the uncoated controls, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The NbTaHfTiZr HEA has received a lot of interests among all RHEAs, since it has a totally disordered BCC solid-solution structure with a melting point of about 1800 °C [,]. At normal temperature and cryogenic temperatures, the NbTaHfTiZr RHEA combines excellent strength and ductility []. The NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA based on this alloy not only maintains excellent room-temperature plasticity but also further improves its strength and has a good cold workability []. In order to explore the potential of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 RHEA for high-temperature applications, it is very necessary to study its mechanical properties at high temperatures. Here, we explore the mechanical properties of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy from RT to 1227 K and analyze its microscopic deformation mechanism. At the same time, we construct the constitutive equation of this alloy through a stress–strain curve in a deformation temperature range of 873–1173 K and a 0.001–0.1 s−1 strain-rate range and quantify the relationship between the strength and temperature.

In the previous results, we found that the crystal structure and microstructure of the alloy did not change significantly after rolling and heat treatment. After discussing the law of strength change with temperature and analyzing the results of the transmission electron microscopy, it is concluded that the deformation of the alloy at high temperature is mainly controlled by dislocation, and the morphology and density of the dislocation control the mechanical properties of the alloy. We have not discussed the plasticity change before, so the next focus is to analyze the change in alloy plasticity at high temperature and the reasons for that change. In high-temperature tensile tests, the strength of the alloy is more important, but the plasticity changes are equally important. In this study, it was obtained that the fracture plasticity of the alloy diminishes as the temperature rises (except at 673 K) (See Figure 4b). This trend is at odds with the experience with alloys in general, and this phenomenon may be the result of the following factors: First, the effect of high-temperature oxidation []. However, only a small number of impurities formed due to oxidation were found upon the fracture, which were not observed in either SEM or TEM observations. This indicates that the oxidative effect was not severe. Second, it may be due to a precipitation at high temperatures. The significant decrease in ductility at 1073 K is similar to that found in the TiZrHfNbTa alloy []. The precipitates from the grain boundary can damage the plasticity of the alloy. However, a previous analysis showed that the alloy had a single-phase BCC structure, and no precipitation was found by TEM. The possible reason is that the size of these precipitates was small, only a few nanometers in size, and it took a considerable time to find them in the field of view of TEM. This phenomenon will be the subject of another study. AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

frame.system: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr in its as‐cast condition
frame.goal: Overcome the alloy’s poor oxygen resistance at high temperature while maintaining its favorable mechanical properties (i.e., room‐temperature tensile ductility of 8–16% and high-temperature yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C).
frame.limitation: Poor oxygen resistance that limits practical high-temperature use.
constraints: Only a single intervention is permitted
Intervention must not sacrifice the alloy’s useful mechanical performance (ductility and yield strength)
Retain the cast processing state (i.e., no extensive thermomechanical processing)
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions (around 1000 °C) in oxidizing atmospheres at strain rates ranging from 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1, with exposure durations defined by application requirements (e.g., prolonged exposure relevant to service conditions).
prior_attempts: Using the untreated cast alloy directly, which results in poor oxygen resistance despite acceptable room-temperature ductility and high-temperature strength.
Attempts to modify the bulk composition to improve oxidation resistance typically lead to adverse changes in mechanical properties, which do not meet the constraint of retaining performance.
frame.understanding: The intervention must provide an effective oxygen barrier and mitigate oxygen diffusion into the alloy without altering the internal microstructure that governs its mechanical performance. The mechanism is expected to involve the formation of a protective, adherent oxide scale that limits further oxidation during service.
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention of applying a thin, high-temperature stable, alumina-forming coating (e.g., via pack cementation or physical vapor deposition of a submicron Al-rich layer) to the cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy. This coating will rapidly form a stable Al2O3 scale upon initial heating, acting as an effective oxygen barrier during high-temperature operation without compromising the bulk alloy’s ductility or strength. The predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr is enhanced oxidation resistance while maintaining the mechanical performance. The validation test should be conducted at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere with exposure times mimicking service conditions (e.g., 100–500 hours) under strain rates of 10^−4 to 10^−2 s^−1. Supporting prior evidence includes literature on diffusion barrier coatings and alumina-forming alloys used in high-temperature applications. A controlled falsification experiment would involve comparing treated and untreated samples under identical conditions to show that the treated alloy exhibits significantly lower oxygen uptake and oxidation-induced degradation while retaining its mechanical properties.

decision.trend: Early studies on refractory high‐entropy and medium‐entropy alloys (including variants of HfNbTaTiZr) focused on tuning bulk composition and microstructure through subtraction methods and thermomechanical treatments to enhance high‐temperature strength and room‐temperature ductility. These works established the sensitivity of mechanical performance to elemental makeup and phase distribution but noted that modifying the bulk to improve oxidation resistance (often attempted via adding oxidation‐resistant elements) tends to compromise the desirable mechanical properties. In essence, while bulk and processing modifications have successfully improved strength and ductility at high temperatures, the oxidation issue has remained an unsolved problem.
decision.unsolved: How to provide an effective oxygen barrier to the as‐cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy during high-temperature oxidation without altering its intrinsic microstructure and thereby its favorable ductility and yield strength.
decision.lever: application of a thin, high-temperature stable, alumina-forming coating (deposited via pack cementation or physical vapor deposition to form a submicron Al-rich layer)
decision.why: This intervention directly addresses the oxygen ingress challenge by forming a protective Al2O3 scale upon initial heating. It follows the trend of avoiding bulk composition changes that impair mechanical properties and leverages the proven effectiveness of diffusion barrier coatings in high-temperature alloys to ensure that the cast alloy’s microstructure—and hence its mechanical performance—remains intact.
